question: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of adverb of degree.
option_1: Karan finished the race with great pride.
option_3: Karan finished the race in the stadium.
option_4: Karan finished the race extremely quickly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Karan finished the race extremely quickly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 4 is correct. An adverb of degree tells how much or to what extent, and it usually modifies an adjective or another adverb. In Option 4, "extremely" modifies the adverb "quickly", so it shows the degree of speed.

◦ Correct sentence: Karan finished the race extremely quickly.

 

• Each of the other three options contains a different kind of adverbial, explained below.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "with great pride" — this is a phrase of manner (it tells how Karan finished), not of degree.

 

• Option 2: "yesterday" — this is an adverb of time, not of degree.

 

• Option 3: "in the stadium" — this is a phrase of place, not of degree.

 

NOTE

 

• degree adverbs: very, quite, too, so, extremely, almost, fairly, rather, enough — they answer "how much?" and normally come before the adjective or adverb they modify (except enough, which comes after it).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The archer aimed carefully, (a)/ and the arrow flew straightly (b)/ towards the target (c)/ at great speed. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Straight" is used both as an adjective and as an adverb, and as an adverb it keeps the same form (it does not take "-ly"). So "straightly" in part (b) must be "straight".

◦ Corrected sentence: The archer aimed carefully, and the arrow flew straight towards the target at great speed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The archer aimed carefully," is a proper subject and verb, with "carefully" as the correct adverb of manner.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "towards the target" is a proper prepositional phrase of direction.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "at great speed." is a proper prepositional phrase of manner.

 

NOTE

 

• Adverbs with the same form as the adjective: fast, hard, late, early, straight — run fast, work hard, arrive late, go straight; never fastly or straightly.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The students couldn't hardly (a)/ concentrate on the lecture (b)/ because of the (c)/ noise from the road. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Hardly" already has a negative meaning (= almost not), so it cannot be used with another negative such as "couldn't / can't / didn't". The double negative is wrong, so "couldn't hardly" must be "could hardly".

◦ Corrected sentence: The students could hardly concentrate on the lecture because of the noise from the road.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "concentrate on the lecture" is proper, with the correct preposition "on" after "concentrate" and the base form after "could".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "because of the" is a proper phrase to show a cause, since "because of" is followed by a noun.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "noise from the road." is a proper noun phrase, with "noise" used as an uncountable noun.

 

NOTE

 

• hardly, scarcely, barely, rarely, seldom are negative in sense, so they are never used with not / n't / never: could hardly concentrate (not couldn't hardly concentrate).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The new waiter (a)/ carried the tray (b)/ clumsy (c)/ and spilled the soup. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "carried" must be described by an adverb (it tells how the tray was carried), and "clumsy" is an adjective. So "clumsy" must be "clumsily" (the "-y" changes to "-i" before "-ly").

◦ Corrected sentence: The new waiter carried the tray clumsily and spilled the soup.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The new waiter" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "carried the tray" is a proper verb and object in the simple past.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and spilled the soup." is a proper compound verb in the simple past, with both verbs sharing the subject "waiter".

 

NOTE

 

• Adjectives ending in "-y" change to "-ily": clumsy → clumsily, easy → easily, happy → happily, angry → angrily, lazy → lazily.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

So severe (a)/ the storm was that (b)/ all flights were cancelled. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with "So + adjective/adverb", the subject and verb are inverted: "So + adjective + verb + subject + that". So "the storm was" in part (b) must be "was the storm".

◦ Corrected sentence: So severe was the storm that all flights were cancelled.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "So severe" is a proper beginning, with the adverb "so" describing the adjective "severe".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "all flights were cancelled." is a proper plural passive verb phrase, agreeing with "flights".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because the missing inversion in part (b) is a mistake.

 

NOTE

 

• So + adjective + was/were/did + subject + that — So heavy was the rain that, So fast did he run that; compare Such was his anger that.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Not only he cheated (a)/ in the exam (b)/ but he also (c)/ lied about it. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with the negative adverbial "Not only", the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion) and the main verb takes its base form. So "Not only he cheated" must be "Not only did he cheat".

◦ Corrected sentence: Not only did he cheat in the exam but he also lied about it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "in the exam" is a proper prepositional phrase of place.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "but he also" is the proper second half of the correlative pair "not only … but also".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "lied about it." is a proper simple past verb phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• Not only + did/does/has + subject + verb … but also — Not only did she sing but she also danced; other inversion triggers: never, seldom, rarely, hardly, scarcely, no sooner, little.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The hikers had climbed (a)/ for four hours (b)/ and had covered (c)/ near ten kilometres. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Near" as an adverb means close (in place or time), while "nearly" means almost. A quantity such as "ten kilometres" needs "almost", so "near ten kilometres" must be "nearly ten kilometres".

◦ Corrected sentence: The hikers had climbed for four hours and had covered nearly ten kilometres.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The hikers had climbed" is a proper past perfect verb, with "climbed" as the correct V3.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "for four hours" is proper, since "for" is used with a period of time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and had covered" is proper, as it is a parallel past perfect verb.

 

NOTE

 

• near (close) — Come near, The station is near; nearly (almost) — nearly ten kilometres, nearly finished.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The rescue team could hard hear the voices trapped under the rubble.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. hardly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• As an adverb, "hard" means with great effort (work hard, try hard), and it does not give the meaning needed here, which is "almost not". The correct adverb is "hardly".

◦ Corrected sentence: The rescue team could hardly hear the voices trapped under the rubble.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "hardy" — this is an adjective meaning strong or tough, so it cannot describe the verb "hear".

 

• Option 2: "hardily" — this is a rare adverb meaning "in a robust manner", and it does not give the sense of "almost not".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "hard" changes the meaning and does not give the required sense of "almost not".

 

NOTE

 

• hard (with effort) — work hard, try hard; hardly (almost not) — can hardly walk, hardly know him.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The young doctor (a)/ likes very much (b)/ classical music (c)/ and plays the sitar. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An adverb of degree such as "very much" must not be placed between the verb and its object. The object "classical music" must come directly after "likes", and the adverb comes at the end: "likes classical music very much".

◦ Corrected sentence: The young doctor likes classical music very much and plays the sitar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The young doctor" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "classical music" is a proper uncountable noun phrase, with no article needed.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and plays the sitar." is a proper simple present verb phrase, with "plays" agreeing with the singular subject.

 

NOTE

 

• She likes tea very much (not likes very much tea); He reads novels regularly; the usual order is verb + object + adverb.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The trainee completes rarely (a)/ his assignments (b)/ on time. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A frequency adverb (always, often, rarely, never, usually) is normally placed before the main verb, and it does not come between the verb and its object. So "completes rarely his assignments" must be "rarely completes his assignments".

◦ Corrected sentence: The trainee rarely completes his assignments on time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "his assignments" is a proper object, with "his" agreeing with the male subject "trainee".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "on time." is a proper idiomatic phrase meaning "punctually".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because the misplaced adverb in part (a) is an error.

 

NOTE

 

• Frequency adverbs go before the main verb (She often visits), after "be" (He is always late) and after the first auxiliary (He has never lied).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The applicant is intelligent, (a)/ but he is (b)/ not enough experienced (c)/ to handle such a project. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adverb "enough" is placed after the adjective or adverb it modifies. So "not enough experienced" must be "not experienced enough".

◦ Corrected sentence: The applicant is intelligent, but he is not experienced enough to handle such a project.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The applicant is intelligent," is a proper singular subject with a linking verb and an adjective.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "but he is" is proper, since "but" correctly joins two contrasting clauses.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "to handle such a project." is a proper infinitive phrase, with "such a" correctly used before a singular noun.

 

NOTE

 

• adjective/adverb + enough — tall enough, fast enough, old enough to vote; but enough comes before a noun: enough money, enough time.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Little he suspected (a)/ that the friendly stranger (b)/ was a detective. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with the negative adverb "Little" (meaning "not at all"), the auxiliary comes before the subject and the main verb takes its base form. So "Little he suspected" must be "Little did he suspect".

◦ Corrected sentence: Little did he suspect that the friendly stranger was a detective.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "that the friendly stranger" is a proper noun clause, with the adjective "friendly" placed before the noun.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "was a detective." is a proper singular verb phrase, with the article "a" before a consonant sound.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because the missing inversion in part (a) is a mistake.

 

NOTE

 

• Little did I know, Little did she realise, Little does he care — "Little" at the beginning of a sentence acts as a negative adverb and needs inversion, like Never, Seldom, Rarely, Hardly.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Scarcely the speaker had begun his speech when the microphone failed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. had the speaker begun.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pattern is "Scarcely / Hardly + had + subject + V3 … when + simple past". When "Scarcely" begins the sentence, the auxiliary "had" comes before the subject, so "the speaker had begun" must be "had the speaker begun".

◦ Corrected sentence: Scarcely had the speaker begun his speech when the microphone failed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "has the speaker begun" — the inversion is right, but the present perfect does not match the past event "failed".

 

• Option 3: "the speaker begun" — the auxiliary is missing, and "begun" alone cannot form a complete verb here.

 

• Option 4: "is the speaker begun" — "is" with "begun" is not a valid verb form here, and it also does not match the past event "failed".

 

NOTE

 

• Scarcely / Hardly / Barely + had + subject + V3 … when; No sooner + had + subject + V3 … than — Hardly had he left when it began to rain.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The team celebrated (a)/ the victory (b)/ so more loudly that the neighbours complained. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "So" is itself an adverb of degree, and it is not combined with a comparative such as "more". So "so more loudly" must be "so loudly".

◦ Corrected sentence: The team celebrated the victory so loudly that the neighbours complained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The team celebrated" is a proper collective noun used as a singular subject with a simple past verb.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the victory" is a proper object with the definite article.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "so more loudly" in part (c) is wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• so loudly that (result) and more loudly than (comparison) are separate patterns — never mix them: so more, more better, most best.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The seminar was (a)/ quiet informative (b)/ and the speakers (c)/ answered every question. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Quiet" is an adjective meaning silent, while "quite" is an adverb of degree meaning "fairly / very". To modify the adjective "informative" we need the adverb, so "quiet informative" must be "quite informative".

◦ Corrected sentence: The seminar was quite informative and the speakers answered every question.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The seminar was" is a proper singular subject with a singular verb.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and the speakers" is a proper plural subject.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "answered every question." is a proper simple past verb phrase, with "every" followed by the singular noun "question".

 

NOTE

 

• quiet (adjective: silent) — a quiet room; quite (adverb: fairly / very) — quite good, quite sure; quit (verb: leave).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The travellers were much tired after the long journey.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. very tired.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Very" is used with adjectives and adverbs in the positive degree (very tired, very slowly), whereas "much" is used with comparatives (much better) and with past participles that work as verbs (much admired). So "much tired" must be "very tired".

◦ Corrected sentence: The travellers were very tired after the long journey.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "tired much" — "much" cannot follow the adjective in this way, so the phrase is wrong.

 

• Option 3: "many tired" — "many" is used only with plural countable nouns, not before an adjective.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "much" cannot be used before the positive adjective "tired".

 

NOTE

 

• very + adjective/adverb (very tall, very slowly); much + comparative (much taller, much better); much + past participle (much appreciated).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The choir leader (a)/ said that no one (b)/ could sing (c)/ as sweet as Meera did. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "sing" must be described by an adverb. So in the pattern "as + adverb + as", "sweet" must be "sweetly".

◦ Corrected sentence: The choir leader said that no one could sing as sweetly as Meera did.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The choir leader" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "said that no one" is a proper reporting clause, and "no one" is a singular pronoun.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "could sing" is proper, with the modal "could" followed by the base form of the verb.

 

NOTE

 

• as + adverb + as describes a verb (sings as sweetly as); as + adjective + as describes a noun (as sweet as honey).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

A young engineer from Pune (a)/ founded the company (b)/ about fifty years before (c)/ and it still thrives today. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Ago" is used with the simple past to count backwards from the present (five years ago). "Before" counts back from another point in the past and is mostly used with the past perfect ("He had left an hour before I came"). So "fifty years before" must be "fifty years ago".

◦ Corrected sentence: A young engineer from Pune founded the company about fifty years ago and it still thrives today.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "A young engineer from Pune" is a proper singular subject, with "a" correctly used before the consonant sound in "young".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "founded the company" is a proper simple past verb phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and it still thrives today." is proper, with "still" before the verb and "thrives" agreeing with "it".

 

NOTE

 

• ago (from now, with the simple past) — He left two hours ago; before (from another past time) — He had left two hours before I arrived.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The patient's condition (a)/ is very better (b)/ today than it was (c)/ yesterday. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Very" is used with positive-degree adjectives and adverbs, and it is not used with comparatives. A comparative such as "better" is strengthened by "much / far / a lot / even / still". So "very better" must be "much better".

◦ Corrected sentence: The patient's condition is much better today than it was yesterday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The patient's condition" is a proper singular subject, with the possessive "patient's".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "today than it was" is proper, since "than" is used with the comparative "better".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "yesterday." is a proper adverb of time.

 

NOTE

 

• much / far / a lot / even / still + comparative (much better, far more costly, even taller); never very better, very taller.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The old man lives (a)/ alone in the hills and (b)/ rarely or ever (c)/ visits the town. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Rarely" and "seldom" are followed by "if ever" (or contrasted with "or never"). The pair "rarely or ever" is not idiomatic, so it must be "rarely, if ever," (or "rarely or never").

◦ Corrected sentence: The old man lives alone in the hills and rarely, if ever, visits the town.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The old man lives" is a proper singular subject with a singular simple present verb.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "alone in the hills and" is proper, with "alone" used as an adverb and "in the hills" as a phrase of place.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "visits the town." is proper, with "visits" agreeing with the singular subject "man".

 

NOTE

 

• rarely / seldom + if ever (He rarely, if ever, complains); rarely / seldom + or never (He rarely or never complains); hardly ever (She hardly ever calls).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The manager has (a)/ already informed (b)/ the staff about the schedule. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. The adverb "already" is correctly placed between the auxiliary "has" and the main verb "informed", and it is properly used in an affirmative sentence.

◦ Sentence as given: The manager has already informed the staff about the schedule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The manager has" is a proper singular subject with the singular auxiliary "has".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "already informed" is proper, with the adverb correctly placed and "informed" as the correct V3.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the staff about the schedule." is proper, since "inform" takes the pattern "inform + person + about + thing".

 

NOTE

 

• Do not over-correct: already is used in affirmative sentences (He has already left), while yet is used in negative and interrogative sentences (He has not left yet, Has he left yet?).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

She has not never (a)/ visited Delhi (b)/ although she (c)/ has lived nearby. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Not" and "never" are both negatives, and two negatives in one clause cancel each other. So "has not never" must be "has never" (or "has not ever").

◦ Corrected sentence: She has never visited Delhi although she has lived nearby.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "visited Delhi" is proper, with V3 after "has" and no preposition needed after "visit".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "although she" is proper, since "although" joins two clauses of contrast.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "has lived nearby." is proper, with a present perfect verb and the adverb "nearby".

 

NOTE

 

• never already has a negative sense: She has never been there (not has not never); similarly nobody, nothing, nowhere, neither, hardly never take another negative.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

She does not (a)/ like spicy food (b)/ and I do not like it too. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a negative sentence, "either" is used to add a similar idea, while "too" is used only in affirmative sentences. So "I do not like it too" must be "I do not like it either".

◦ Corrected sentence: She does not like spicy food and I do not like it either.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "She does not" is proper, with "does" agreeing with the third-person singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "like spicy food" is proper, with the base form "like" after "does not".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "too" in part (c) is wrong in a negative sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• too / also (affirmative) — I like it too; either (negative) — I do not like it either.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The thieves broke into the shop yesterday night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. last night.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The standard expression for the night that has just passed is "last night". "Yesterday" is combined with morning, afternoon and evening (yesterday morning), but not with "night".

◦ Corrected sentence: The thieves broke into the shop last night.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "last of night" — this is not an English expression and has no meaning here.

 

• Option 2: "the yesterday night" — the article "the" cannot be used before "yesterday", and the phrase repeats the same error.

 

• Option 3: No improvement required — incorrect, because "yesterday night" is not standard usage.

 

NOTE

 

• yesterday morning / afternoon / evening but last night (not yesterday night); similarly last week / last month / last year.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Rahul enjoys playing cricket, and so do I.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No substitution required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is correct as it stands. To agree with a positive statement, we use "so + auxiliary + subject", and the auxiliary must match the tense of the first clause. The first clause is in the simple present ("enjoys"), so "so do I" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: Rahul enjoys playing cricket, and so do I.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "have I" — "have" is the auxiliary of the present perfect, but the first clause is in the simple present.

 

• Option 2: "am I" — "am" is a form of "be", but the first clause has the main verb "enjoys", so the matching auxiliary is "do".

 

• Option 3: "does I" — "does" is a third-person singular form and cannot be used with "I".

 

NOTE

 

• so + auxiliary + subject (positive agreement) — so do I, so did she; neither / nor + auxiliary + subject (negative agreement) — neither do I.
